commitResults.messageTitle: Changed chatbot name from duke to turing
Added Echo and Exit functionality Echo - repeats the message sent by the user Exit - If the input from the user is 'bye', program will terminate
Add task storage and list command
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot previously echoed each input and forgot it immediately. Store
inputs so the user can review them later:

* Keep items in a fixed-size String[100] array, which is sufficient because
  the requirements cap the item count at 100. This avoids introducing
  ArrayList before the course covers it.
* Any input that is not a known command is stored and acknowledged with
  "added: <text>"; "list" prints the stored items, numbered from 1.
* Generalise reply() to varargs so a single call can print a multi-line
  response such as the list, keeping the divider formatting in one place.
* Guard against overflowing the array with an explanatory message rather
  than an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Introduce Task class to represent stored items
commitResults.messageBody:
Items were stored as plain Strings, which leaves no room for per-item state
such as whether a task is done. Model a task as an object instead:

* Add Task, holding the description and an isDone flag, with markAsDone(),
  markAsNotDone() and getStatusIcon() for the "[X]" / "[ ]" box.
* Override toString() so the task itself decides how it is displayed; the
  chatbot can concatenate it without knowing about the status box.
* Change the store from String[] to Task[] and add the "Here are the tasks
  in your list:" header to the list output.

This is the A-Classes extension: a class is a more natural fit than parallel
arrays of primitives once each item carries more than one piece of state.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Tasks could be stored and listed but their done status could never change,
so the status box was always empty.

* Recognise "mark <n>" and "unmark <n>", which flip the task's isDone flag
  and echo the updated task back to the user.
* Match on a "mark "/"unmark " prefix rather than equality, since these
  commands carry an argument. "unmark" does not start with "mark", so the
  two branches cannot be confused.
* Extract setDoneStatus() so both commands share one code path, differing
  only by a boolean and the confirmation message.
* Convert the 1-based task number the user sees into a 0-based array index,
  and reject a number that is out of range or not a number at all, instead
  of throwing NumberFormatException or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add skill for SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project must follow the SE-EDU Java coding standard, but the rules
live on an external web page that is not available while coding, so
compliance depends on remembering them.

Capture the intermediate-level rules as the project skill
seedu-java-coding-standard, and mandate it in AGENTS.md so it is
consulted whenever Java code is written or reviewed.

The "put every class in a package" rule is noted as deferred, because
introducing packages is the separate A-Packages increment of this
course project.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add skill for SE-EDU Git conventions
commitResults.messageBody:
Commit messages in this project must follow the SE-EDU Git conventions,
but the rules live on an external web page, so each commit message is
written from memory and the standard drifts.

Capture the commit message and branch naming rules as the project skill
seedu-git-standard, and mandate it in AGENTS.md so it is consulted
before any commit message is written.

Record in the skill that the guide says nothing about tag names, so the
existing project convention of course increment names is kept.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Comply with SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The code predates the adoption of the SE-EDU Java coding standard, so
parts of it do not follow the standard's naming and documentation rules.

Bring the existing code into line with the standard:

- Document main(), which is public and so requires a header comment.
- Capitalise and punctuate the @param and @return descriptions, and drop
  the alignment padding, as the standard shows single-spaced tags.
- Rename the caught exception from e to exception, since only i, j, k,
  m, n, c and d are sanctioned as short scratch names.
- Rename the Scanner from in to scanner, as the variable is in scope for
  the whole of main() and the standard asks for longer names at larger
  scopes.

Behaviour is unchanged; every edit is naming or documentation only.

The rule requiring each class to be in a package is not applied here,
because introducing packages is the separate A-Packages increment.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Make command parsing tolerant of messy input
commitResults.messageBody:
Commands are currently matched against the raw input line with equals
and startsWith, so anything but exact lowercase text with single spaces
is misread. "BYE" and "  list  " fall through to the add branch and are
stored as tasks, "mark  2" is parsed as the argument " 2", and a stray
Enter adds an empty task to the list.

Normalize each line before dispatching on it: trim it and collapse runs
of whitespace into single spaces, split off the first word as the
command word, and compare that word with equalsIgnoreCase. Doing the
cleanup once at the point of input keeps the rest of the code free of
whitespace handling, and matching on the command word alone means the
argument no longer has to be recovered with substring arithmetic.

Blank lines now get a prompt to type something instead of becoming a
task, "mark" with no number reuses the existing "tell me the task
number" message, and listing an empty list says so rather than printing
a bare header.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Record the SLAP guideline in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md states the coding standard and the Git conventions this project
follows, but says nothing about code quality. SLAP, the Single Level of
Abstraction Principle, is one of the guidelines the course expects the
code to follow, so it has to be written down somewhere an assistant will
always read.

Add a "Code quality: SLAP" section stating the principle, a short
bad/good example, and the one case where two levels of abstraction are
acceptable.

State the rule in AGENTS.md itself rather than in the
seedu-java-coding-standard skill, because that skill mirrors a single
upstream page (the SE-EDU Java coding standard) and SLAP comes from a
different source, the textbook's "Code Quality" chapter. Keeping the
mirror faithful makes it easy to re-check against upstream later.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add todo, deadline and event task types
commitResults.messageBody:
Every stored item is currently a plain Task holding nothing but a
description, so the chatbot cannot record that a report is due on Sunday
or that a meeting runs from 2pm to 4pm. The user has no way to say which
kind of task is being added either: any unrecognized line is stored
verbatim.

Make Task abstract and give it an abstract type icon, then add the three
concrete subclasses Todo, Deadline and Event. Each subclass supplies its
own icon, and Deadline and Event extend toString to append their
date/time details to the text built by the superclass. Add the matching
todo, deadline and event commands, which split their argument on /by,
/from and /to.

Making Task abstract means the compiler now rejects a task with no type,
which is why unrecognized input is answered with a list of the known
commands instead of being stored as a bare task. Dates and times are
kept as free text, as the increment allows, so "no idea :-p" is as
acceptable as "Sunday".

Move the task list into fields and split the command handling out of
main, so that main reads as the outline of the program rather than a
mix of high-level steps and parsing detail, per SLAP. The separators are
matched case insensitively and tolerate missing spaces, in keeping with
the input handling added earlier.

commitResults.messageTitle: Simplify the deadline and event argument parsing
commitResults.messageBody:
addEvent decides whether the user supplied every part with a four-term
boolean expression, fed by a ternary that substitutes an empty array when
"/from" is missing. The empty array is a sentinel standing for "no split
happened", which the reader has to infer from the length check further
down, and the parts are validated all at once, after both splits.

Extract splitAtSeparator, which returns the two parts of one split or
null when the separator is absent or a part is blank, and have addEvent
call it twice behind a guard clause each time.

The code quality guidelines ask that complicated expressions be evaluated
in steps and that the reader not be 'tripped up' by things that look
similar but are not. Splitting once per call and checking the outcome
immediately removes both the sentinel and the compound condition, and
leaves the happy path unindented at the end of the method. addDeadline
performed the same split-and-validate work inline, so it now shares the
helper instead of repeating it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a TaskList class to hold the stored tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
The task array and the count of entries in use are two static fields
shared by five methods. Every one of them reaches into that state
directly, so the fields act as global variables: nothing in a method
signature says which methods read or write the list, and the
translation between the task numbers shown to the user and array
indexes is repeated wherever the array is indexed.

Move the array and the count into a TaskList class that exposes add,
getTask, hasTaskNumber, isEmpty, isFull and getTaskCount, and hold one
TaskList in an instance field of Turing, created by main.

The guidelines ask that the scope of variables be minimized and global
variables avoided, because they create implicit links between the code
segments that share them. The task list is now reachable only through
the object that owns it, and the off-by-one adjustment lives in
TaskList.getTask instead of at each call site. TaskList takes task
numbers as the user sees them, starting at 1, so the surrounding code
no longer switches between two numbering schemes. Only the constants
and the helpers that touch no task state stay static, which is now a
reliable signal that those methods hold nothing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Represent the commands as an enum instead of loose strings
commitResults.messageBody:
The first word of the user's input can only be one of seven commands,
but that set is written down as seven unrelated String constants and
recognized by a chain of seven equalsIgnoreCase calls. Nothing ties the
constants together as one set of alternatives, and the message shown for
an unrecognized command spells the same seven words out again in prose,
so adding a command means remembering to update a sentence that the
compiler does not check.

Add a Command enum holding each command with the keyword that invokes
it, look the keyword up once with Command.fromKeyword, and dispatch on
the result with a switch.

The guidelines recommend an enumeration wherever a variable can take
only a small number of finite values, since it states the alternatives
explicitly rather than leaving them implied by a series of comparisons.
Command.getKeywords now builds the list of commands offered to the user
from the enum itself, so that message cannot drift out of step. Matching
without regard to capitalization moves into the enum, where it applies
to every command at once, and the switch uses arrow labels, which cannot
fall through from one case to the next. Its default branch handles
unrecognized input, which is the genuine 'everything else' case rather
than the last of the alternatives.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the indent used when a reply shows a task
commitResults.messageBody:
The two spaces that indent a task shown inside a reply appear as a bare
" " literal at three call sites, where nothing marks them as one shared
formatting decision rather than three coincidental strings. Alongside
them, the mark and unmark branches differ only in the sentence they
report, yet each repeats the whole reply call.

Introduce a TASK_INDENT constant and have setDoneStatus choose its
sentence in the branches, then issue a single reply after them.

The guidelines ask that magic literals be avoided in general, not only
magic numbers, and that duplication be kept to a minimum. The indent now
has a name that says what it is for, and changing it is one edit rather
than three consistent ones. Reporting from a single place also leaves
the branches showing only what actually differs between marking and
unmarking.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop two comments that restate the code
commitResults.messageBody:
Two comments describe mechanics the code already shows: one spells out
what the regular expression "\s+" matches, on a line whose Javadoc
already says the method collapses runs of whitespace, and one announces
that a Scanner reads input line by line, directly above the call to
nextLine that shows exactly that.

Delete both.

The guidelines ask that comments explain what the code is for and why it
is written that way, rather than how it works, and that they not repeat
what is already obvious. The remaining comments all carry a rationale a
reader could not recover from the code alone, such as why the separators
are regular expressions and why each split is limited to two parts, so
removing these two makes the surviving comments more worth reading.

commitResults.messageTitle: Escape the command placeholders in Javadoc
commitResults.messageBody:
The Javadoc for addDeadline and addEvent shows the shape each command
takes as "<task> /by <when>" and "<task> /from <start> /to <end>". Angle
brackets open an HTML tag in Javadoc, so a tool that renders these
comments, such as the quick documentation popup in an IDE, drops every
placeholder and shows the shape as "/by" and "/from /to" instead. The
one detail these sentences exist to convey is the part that disappears.

Wrap both in {@code}, which reproduces the text literally.

The guidelines ask that comments be written for the reader. A comment
that renders as something other than what was written misleads the very
reader it was aimed at, and {@code} is also how the coding standard
marks up code fragments appearing in documentation.
